subject: chemistry
title: Chemical bonds and types of structure
key_idea: There are three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic. Ionic bonding joins metals to non-metals. Covalent bonding joins non-metal atoms. Metallic bonding holds metal atoms together. The bonding and structure decide a substance's properties.

blocks.text: Every bond is an electrostatic force acting between particles. The three types differ in which particles are involved and what happens to the electrons.

items.meaning: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed by transfer of electrons.
Strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.

rows: Compounds of a metal with a non-metal
Most non-metal elements and compounds of non-metals
Positive metal ions and delocalised electrons

items: Electrons are transferred in ionic bonding and shared in covalent and metallic bonding.
Argon does not form compounds because its atoms have a full outer shell. They do not share or transfer electrons.

diagram.alt: Sort each substance by its type of bonding.
diagram.prompt: Which type of bonding holds each substance together?

items: Metal with non-metal: ionic. Non-metal with non-metal: covalent. Metal elements and alloys: metallic.
All three are electrostatic forces and involve transferring or sharing electrons.

blocks.text: The type of bonding gives four types of structure. You can identify one from its properties.

diagram.alt: Ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent and metallic structures compared.
items: Ionic
Simple molecular
Giant covalent
Metallic
**Simple molecular** substances have low melting points because little energy is needed to overcome the weak forces between molecules.
**Giant** structures have high melting points because a lot of energy is needed to break many strong bonds or overcome strong forces.
Ionic compounds conduct when molten or dissolved because the ions are free to move. They do not conduct as solids because the ions are fixed in place.
Metals conduct because delocalised electrons can move through the structure.
Many ionic compounds dissolve in water. Giant covalent substances and metals do not.
Polymers have strong covalent bonds within their chains and weak intermolecular forces between chains. They have low melting points, do not conduct and can be flexible.
Atoms themselves do not have the bulk properties of a material. Melting point and conductivity belong to the whole structure.
Low melting point and no conduction: simple molecular.
High melting point and conducts only when molten or dissolved: ionic.
High melting point and conducts when solid: metallic.

checks.q: Name the type of bonding in a compound formed between a metal and a non-metal.
Describe the structure and bonding in a metal.
checks.a: Positive metal ions in a lattice, surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons, with strong forces of attraction between the ions and the electrons.

checks.q: Ammonia (NH3) has a boiling point of -33 °C. Silicon dioxide has a boiling point of 2230 °C. Explain the difference.
checks.a: Ammonia is simple molecular with weak intermolecular forces. Silicon dioxide is giant covalent with strong covalent bonds. More energy is needed to break the bonds in silicon dioxide than the intermolecular forces in ammonia.

exam_phrases: (atoms of) argon have a stable arrangement of electrons
(atoms of) argon have a full outer shell (of electrons)
(so) argon (atoms) do not share / transfer electrons

mistakes.wrong: Argon does not form compounds because it does not want to react.
mistakes.right: Say argon atoms have a full outer shell, a stable arrangement of electrons, so they do not share or transfer electrons.

mistakes.wrong: The type of bonding in ClF3 is intermolecular forces.
mistakes.right: The bonding is covalent, because both elements are non-metals. Intermolecular forces are ignored.

worked_example.question:
Argon has the atomic number 18.

Explain why argon does not form compounds.

Answer in terms of electrons.
answer_points: Argon atoms have a stable arrangement of electrons (a full outer shell).
So argon atoms do not share or transfer electrons.
worked_example.tip: One mark each. Link the full outer shell to atoms not sharing or transferring electrons.

exam_phrases: more energy to break bonds in silicon dioxide than intermolecular forces in ammonia
metal ions surrounded by delocalised electrons
strong forces of attraction between delocalised electrons and metal ions
needs lots of energy to separate the particles

mistakes.wrong: Silicon dioxide has a high boiling point because it is ionic.
mistakes.right: Silicon dioxide is giant covalent. Ionic is rejected, because both elements are non-metals.

mistakes.wrong: Metals have high melting points because of intermolecular forces between atoms.
mistakes.right: Mentioning intermolecular forces, covalent bonding, molecules or ionic bonding limits the answer to 1 mark. Use metal ions, delocalised electrons and strong forces of attraction.

mistakes.wrong: A giant covalent structure has strong bonds.
mistakes.right: 'Strong bonds' alone is ignored. State a property that follows from the structure, such as a high melting point, hardness or not conducting.

worked_example.question:
Ammonia, NH3, and silicon dioxide, SiO2, are both compounds that are made of two non-metallic elements.
Ammonia has a boiling point of –33 °C.
Silicon dioxide has a boiling point of 2230 °C.
Explain why the boiling points of ammonia and silicon dioxide are so different.
answer_points: Ammonia is simple molecular, with weak intermolecular forces.
Silicon dioxide is giant covalent, with strong covalent bonds.
More heat or energy is needed to break the bonds in silicon dioxide than the intermolecular forces in ammonia.
worked_example.tip: The marks are independent. Do not describe either substance as ionic.

exam_phrases: positive (metal) ions in a lattice surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons
strong forces of attraction between ions and electrons
ionic: high melting point, conducts when molten or dissolved but not as a solid
intermolecular forces in bromine are weak
covalent bonds in diamond require a lot of energy to break
polymers: low melting point, do not conduct, can be flexible

mistakes.wrong: Metals have a structure of ionic and covalent bonds.
mistakes.right: Any reference to ionic or covalent bonding or intermolecular forces scores 0 for the structure of a metal. Say positive ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons.

mistakes.wrong: Metals conduct because they have free ions.
mistakes.right: Free ions score 0. Say metals have electrons that can move, or delocalised electrons.

mistakes.wrong: Bromine has a low melting point because its covalent bonds are weak.
mistakes.right: The covalent bonds are not broken. Say the intermolecular forces in bromine are weak and need less energy to break.

worked_example.question:
The table shows the type of bonding in three substances.
Substance | Type of bonding
Bromine, Br2 | simple molecular (covalent)
Sodium chloride, NaCl | ionic
Diamond, C | giant covalent

Describe and compare the types of bonding in these three substances.
Predict which substance will have the lowest melting point.
answer_points: Sodium chloride (ionic): strong electrostatic forces between ions need a lot of energy to break.
Diamond (giant covalent): many strong covalent bonds need a lot of energy to break.
Bromine (simple molecular): intermolecular forces are weak and need less energy to break.
Bromine has the lowest melting point. Sodium chloride and diamond have higher melting points.
worked_example.tip: This is a six-mark answer marked by level. Describe each bonding type, link it to the melting point, then predict bromine.
